title: Three unannounced 'Aurora' models surface in OpenAI's API with no documentation
subtitle: aurora-red-alpha, aurora-green-alpha, and aurora-blue-alpha appeared on October 17 and were spotted the next day — one returns 503 capacity errors instead of 404s, hinting at a backend wiring quietly in place.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Three undocumented model IDs appeared in OpenAI's API: aurora-red-alpha, aurora-green-alpha, and aurora-blue-alpha. Independent researcher Andrew Curran flagged them on X on October 18. Creation timestamps point to October 17, roughly 26 hours before anyone noticed. OpenAI has published nothing — no changelog entry, no documentation, no pricing. aurora-red-alpha is returning 503 capacity errors rather than 404s, which suggests the backend route is wired up and quota-limited rather than merely missing. The other two still return 404s. TestingCatalog reports the IDs were pulled soon after public attention arrived and characterizes it as a rollout mistake.

The mechanism to watch is route-exists versus route-wired. A 404 means the API has never heard of the model; a 503 means the service exists but can't serve you right now. The latter is what you see when a new model is deployed behind a gate and someone forgot to disable the public code path. That pattern has preceded several past OpenAI launches, including image models and codex variants, so an aurora-alpha reveal in the next few weeks would not be surprising.

Speculation on purpose is split. Earlier in the year an OpenRouter model called aurora-alpha turned out to be GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark, which argues for a coding or fast-inference release. More recent arena tests reportedly saw aurora identifiers producing images, which would align with a GPT-Image-3 generation. OpenAI has released neither public confirmation nor denial. Treat the leak as a signal that something ships soon — not as evidence of what it is.

A note for learners: unannounced identifiers in a production API are a developer-relations tool as much as an accident. They let the lab test latency and errors against real traffic, and they generate anticipation. If you build on OpenAI, add a periodic script that lists available models — you will see new names before the blog post, and you can plan integration work before competitors.
